definition: Near v. Minnesota, 283 U.S. 697 (1931), is a landmark Supreme Court case revolving around the First Amendment. The Court held that prior restraint on publication violated the First Amendment. This holding had a broader impact on free speech generally. The case was brought by a Minnesota public official against Near, who published in The Saturday Press, under a Minnesota State statute that allowed for temporary and permanent injunctions against those who created a public nuisance, by publishing, selling, or distributing a “malicious, scandalous and defamatory newspaper.” After an ex parte hearing, the state court granted an injunction against The Saturday Press. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed, and Near appealed to the United States Supreme Court. In a 5-4 decision, the Supreme Court reversed the judgment and held that prior restraint of the press is unconstitutional. The First Amendment protects citizens' freedom of speech from the federal government’s censorship. The Supreme Court used the Fourteenth Amendment (incorporation doctrine) to apply the First Amendment to state governments. The Supreme Court reasoned that the relevant statute allowing prior restraint could lead to a system of complete censorship under the guise of preventing public nuisance. The Minnesota statute required publications to defend the nuisance claim by showing “good motives and justifiable ends” for their content, or risk censorship. However, under the First Amendment, even if the liberty of press is abused by “miscreant purveyors” of scandal, it “does not make any less necessary the immunity of the press from previous restraint in dealing with official misconduct.” The Court stressed that as a general principle that neither the federal nor any state government could censor publications in advance of exceptional cases.
